claim: For all complex polynomials of degree 2 or 3, the intersection of convex hulls of critical-level root fibers equals the derivative root hull; an explicit rational quartic violates equality.

correctness.rationale: For all p of degree 2 the sole derivative zero is the sole critical-level root. For cubic p with a double derivative zero the centered normal form is a pure cube. With distinct derivative zeros b±u, the general normal form p(b+t)=a(t^3-3u^2t)+c factors at each critical value as a(t-u)^2(t+2u) or a(t+u)^2(t-2u), yielding collinear segments [b-2u,b+u] and [b-u,b+2u] whose intersection is [b-u,b+u]. For the specific quartic, p′=4(z+8/5)(z^2+1), so its derivative hull is in Re z<=0. The exact three critical-level factorizations contain w=2/21 through convex combinations with weights 89/112, 9/14 and 5/14; the positive real witness lies outside the derivative hull. An independent SymPy program checked all three polynomial factorizations, all three barycentric identities, and both generic cubic polynomial identities, with no inference from finite examples to the universal claim.

methodology_note: Analytical proof reviewed independently of symbolic checker; symbolic computation verifies exact polynomial identities only. No external expert or formal proof attestation is asserted.

evidence: Rüdinger 2014 Theorem 2.1 and Theorem 3.1 locate critical points using triangles or sectors of a single polynomial’s zero hull; no additive critical-level fibers appear.

evidence: The fiber hull at a critical point q is conv(p^{-1}(p(q))), equivalently K_{-p(q)}; Gauss-Lucas only gives K′ subset each such hull.

equivalent_formulations.reasoning: Finite sampling at all critical values is a different quantifier from either all additive shifts or a single unshifted hull. Even an all-shift identity would not force equality after removing most shifts; the proof and counterexample here do not rely on the withdrawn theorem.

value.rationale: The critical values are a canonical finite family of shifts when attempting to recover the derivative-zero convex hull from fiber-zero convex hulls. Proving the exact low-degree success and providing the first rational quartic obstruction identifies a motivated sharp boundary that is useful when deciding whether that finite sampling shortcut is valid. The result does not classify quartic failures, cover degrees above four, or resolve an arbitrary-shifts intersection identity.
